full_text:
Interviewer:	The questions I’ve got today are about how you’re getting on on placement, and how you think it relates to your course and things like that. And there’s a few questions about gender stuff as well. So when did you start working for [company]?

Subject:	When did I start here? It would have been middle of July last year.

Interviewer:	OK. Can you tell me a bit about what [company] do?

Subject:	OK. This division sort of deals with like power generation really, so energy also covers wind power and what else? Sorry, I can only think gas turbines at the moment, power generators because that’s what they do here. This site specifically comes under inspection and repair and this workshop inspects and repairs gas turbines in different frame sizes all across Europe and part of the Midland East as well. Gas turbines are used mainly for power generation, industrial applications and just like the national grid and stuff.

Interviewer:	How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	It's relaxed, you don't feel any pressure at all, obviously like at this site particularly because it’s a workshop there are a lot of men about, but you don't feel excluded or at an advantage in any way, it is a relaxed place here. I don't know if you would have the same kind of environment like in a more corporate position, but here it’s really relaxed. 

Interviewer:	Ok I have got some more questions about that later. (Ok.) How useful do you think your degree has been so far in the work that you are doing?

Subject:	At the moment I haven't really had to use anything that I learnt from my degree. Maybe how I apply myself to doing jobs, like the organisation and keeping your focus and like the self-motivation thing which is kind of common with the degree as well because it is a bit hardcore, if I can say that. But that's because at the moment I'm in the more commercial role, but because I'm from an engineering background I want to get involved in more production stuff, so I’m going to spend some time with the guys and learn a bit more about the turbine itself and the components, which I have done already, but there's always more to learn. So I'd say at the moment, not much.

Interviewer:	Is there anything that you wish you had learned at uni before you started the placement?

Subject:	In order to help me here? (Yes) Not really apart from I could have made myself a bit more familiar with AutoCad ‘cos that seems to be a popular programme used in the industry. But I don’t think they could have prepared me any better course wise or just personal skills wise, I think it’s just … Luckily it's one of those environments where it's good to be in that situation and learn what’s going on there.

Interviewer:	Did you do anything about Health and Safety at Uni?

Subject:	We might have done it briefly when we did our projects and we had to be involved in the workshop. I don’t think there was massive training.

Interviewer:	Have you had to do a lot of Health and Safety stuff here?

Subject:	Yes. On my first day here we did Health and Safety, just in order to say that we could go on the shop floor. We couldn’t go anywhere without it. And recently we've been on the site, and because certain companies have their own on site Health and Safety you have to go through that before you can be allowed on the site, especially if you're going unescorted.

Interviewer:	Do you think the Health and Safety stuff you learnt at uni helped when you got here?

Subject:	I think it's pretty much the same, but I suppose maybe there's greater risk on site because you're actually dealing with the actual turbines. They're going to tweak it somehow, so it's not going to change that much, but I think Health and Safety its one of those things that just because you've done it once doesn’t mean you should forget it. It should be done all the time, so that's not a problem at all, even if when you go through that with me its good to know it when you're in the actual environment.

Interviewer:	Ok. How did you find the transition from education to work?

Subject:	Not a problem it was fine, I think because I did a foundation year I’d done an extra year at college I think I needed the year out just to see where it would all go, even though I haven’t really used much of what I’ve learnt so far. But, to see like an industry that actually involves engineering, it makes a change from just reading the text books all the time. (Yes) Its good to see it.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve had to face any new issues at all, like dealing with different types of people or office politics, anything like that?

Subject:	It's been fine. I think it's good in a sense that depending on how you’re going to react to it, you'll learn a way of how to deal with it. Either you will stay focussed on what you're doing and not get involved in it, or you might be of the character that, you know, will get involved in it. I haven’t, I’ve been able to stay focused. You just get used to it really. So, what’s the word? You're not as vulnerable to the situation; you wise up to it and also, yes definitely, dealing with differently types of people. There are some people that might have the same background as you university wise, used to working in groups, just a different approach to things, and then obviously you've got the workshop guys that have a different set of skills, and knowing how to talk to everyone and deal with everyone, and not expecting them to, kind of like be psychic really, do you know what I mean? It’s just learning to deal with it. I don't think that's an element that you can get away or not get anywhere. Any new environment that you're , even though you've dealt with it before and you have those skills, you’re tested once again, so the test really is to keep doing it. But it’s never been a problem really.

Interviewer:	Ok. How do you feel about going back to uni?

Subject:	I'm really not looking forward to doing exams, it's been nice, the fact that - I don't know if my focus is better, but at work for the duration that you’re here, you can focus on work and at least you get that chance to switch off when you go home or at the weekends and at uni it just seems to be a never ending, up-hill struggle sometimes, so I'm enjoying having my year out kind of thing, and when it comes back to October, I will just deal with it then. I am not going to speed up the process. I want to enjoy my experience here.

Interviewer:	Ok What do you think are the main ways that work and university differ?

Subject:	In a way the deadlines, like something - whether you’ve have a long time to work on it or something’s come up like when units have gone through (forced altitude?) you need to, that’s like when they have had to shut them down unexpectedly, and certain information is needed on the spot. Well obviously like at uni you do have coursework and things but you kind of know how long you've got to do it. Yes like I said the fact that with work you can kind of leave work at work. You can switch off, you can actually leave. You feel as though you can detach from the situation and come back to work refreshed. I think your focus is better then as well because you're not thinking about it all time. Also I think in the workplace it's a lot to do with how you interact with people. We do get the opportunity to do a lot of teamwork or group work at uni, but it's just not the same. I can appreciate what they were trying to do and I’d still encourage them to do it, but in the workplace it's a totally different system.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is?

Subject:	I've thought about it, I think at university it seems like a real chore, a real hassle to work in a group, and at work it just seems like you've got this common goal, you are just trying to get each others ideas and obviously some people might know certain information and you need to retrieve that from them. And it does seem like you're working together like really with your aims in the same kind of framework. Yes the only way I can describe it in uni is like a chore. You think 'oh not group work again’ you think that can do it better in your own time by yourself, it would be great kind of thing. You don't have to be bothered with meetings and things like that whereas at work you've got to say (inaudible) in the same places, you do have other commitments, and it might be workplace, it might be outside but at work you can appreciate meetings more, getting together churning out your ideas, going away. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	So you think at work you maybe have clearer roles within your teams?

Subject:	Yes. You pick up on like peoples skills and say yes they know how to best go about something or they know where to find out certain information. Yes, it is much easier, not that it’s discussed that ‘yes, you’ll do this and you’ll do this’, but it is clearer.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there is anyway that group work at uni could be redesigned to reflect industry?

Subject:	I don't know. At uni there seems to be more of a competitive edge, everybody, even though you are working in a group, the competitiveness is there more than in the workplace and there's always someone trying to be the leader to lead the group, instead of how about everyone just taking even responsibility, so I can't think how you could implement that but from the group work that I have done, I think that’s probably one of the things that could make team work more effective.

Interviewer:	So do you think that you’ve found being at uni is a more competitive environment?

Subject:	Yes definitely.

Interviewer:	Do you still think that there are benefits from doing group work at uni? 

Subject:	Yeah. You do need to know how to work with people that aren't just your friends and you say 'oh do you know I'm going to have a lie in, can you do that for me' definitely needs to be done. I'd suggest it would be really good if students doing it got a chance to do a placement, went ahead a did a placement to really see where it fits in. Because I think probably in a uni environment you might think that you get on well with people, but in a work situation, you are actually thrown together, you can't really afford to have conflict that you would normally and fly off the handle. It’s really not like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think you will get on better working in a group when you go back?

Subject:	Yes. Well last year I found myself getting really frustrated at things, like trying to get your point across and then obviously if you've got someone that's really strong about their view about something. Whereas yeah definitely here you feel you can give your idea, it can be reviewed and it's a bit fairer. I still think there is competitiveness here, because you've got your production people and your commercial people and there's a bit of a battle between them 'Oh you haven't passed me the right information on’ and that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Is that between departments then? (Yes.) Ok. Do [company] employ many women here then?

Subject:	They do employ women, I don't know whether you'd regard it as many. I'll see if I can count – I believe it might be 5, but let me check. Possibly 6, but I'd say 3 of those are more of an admin position, 1 just happens to be another student, but then again she's coming in from a marketing economics background. A student just like me. There's another lady here she was at, she did a degree in material science, but she's still in a commercial role and then there's myself. So yes they do employ them, but not really.

Interviewer:	Ok. Do the company have a structure or programme in place for placement students to follow?

Subject:	In terms of you are given responsibility, there is a job to do, it might be assisting one of the managers with what they do. You have the responsibility of checking out details of things but it's not too structured, which is a good thing because there's a lot of stuff that's going on here and it is a big organisation and if there is anything that you find interesting and want to get involved in, all you have to do is say and it can happen, so that is good. I think it's important that you've got the interest there. You kind of go into your placement knowing what you want to take out from it. It can be like a brief thing it doesn't have to be so specific ‘I want to learn how to use that piece of equipment’, but you need some sort of plan when you go for it, and I think that, it's 50/50 that the company put a structure there for you but also for you to be able to say actually, I think I'd benefit more from this, you know I've not giving it my best or you’re not getting the best out of me while I'm stuck here.

Interviewer:	Do you have appraisals or anything like that?

Subject:	No, but my Commercial Manager, he's based up in Scotland cos’ he works from home, but when he's down he always takes, say half an hour, sometimes even more, to find out how you’re doing, if there’s anything that’s bothering you, if there's anything that you want to do. Its not really an appraisal but there is kind of that check up on you to make sure that you're not just sat here bawling your eyes because your bored like rigid kind of thing. 

Interviewer:	Ok. Has your role in the company involved what you expected?

Subject:	I don’t know, in a way no, I thought I'd thought I'd be learning a bit more about the technology, a bit more about the engineering side of things. It's difficult here cos’ most of the engineering is done out in the States and here it's mainly processing and production and things like that, but even on a production level there's a lot to learn from it, so that's why I really really want to get into that side. Initially it didn't bother me too much because obviously a new environment, I've not been in like this kind of industry before, and you're trying to get to grips with your job and the ways of doing things, so I was quite happy just to do that. At the same time I did like have an interest in coming down on the shop floor and enquire myself. At the beginning it wasn't so specific, not that they hadn't planned what to do for me as a role, but in a way that flexibility is there. But I think I would have like to spend a bit more time on the production side of things.

Interviewer:	Ok. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

Subject:	Definitely not too little. I'd say, yes, not to feel the pressure wise, but no definitely, like yes there’s certain jobs that you’re left to kind of take care of. Obviously people are about if you need to ask questions, you don't feel as though you have to go through it alone and if something goes wrong it’s all your fault.

Interviewer:	So you feel like you’re in a supportive environment?

Subject:	Yes definitely. I think that for the experience that we have, just coming in from university, it's not an insulting level of like responsibility but I think it’s a good level.

Interviewer:	Ok. How would you summarise the experience so far then?

Subject:	So far? I'm definitely glad that I've done it. I think I wouldn't have been able to take from it if I'd just stayed at university. Now I realise, I wasn’t of the idea of doing a placement anyway, but I think it's just as valuable as doing your degree and it's one thing knowing all the stuff, which is great, but being able to apply it and communicate that across to people is so important and even how you deal with things in certain environments where maybe previously you would have like got annoyed so it's a lot to do with how you respond to things, how you go about - yes personal things. And also it gives you more confidence, because a lot of the time like particularly at uni, well anywhere really, you always feel as though there's always going to be someone doing a better job than you are, and at uni I think the pressure really is there obviously because you really think that you're trying your hardest and maybe it's just the way that you're applying yourself to it. Yes you can really put the pressure on yourself a lot, and being here, in a way uses all your skills, not just what you've learned out of a text book or at a lecture, but how you are as a person, it's like you're using one hundred per cent of you more or less. The confidence that you can take from that when you're going back into your final year I think it will help a lot.

Interviewer:	So it’s been a positive experience? 

Subject:	Yes definitely.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

Subject:	Drawbacks? The only drawbacks, I suppose it depends on the type of person is they’re going to look on it as being an extra year at uni or if they don’t have the - what's the word - I can't think of the word but if your like in your placement, you're not exactly stimulated but you need to find areas or see how you going to solve this problem, how you’re going to motivate yourself. 'What is there that’s going to interest me?' I think I've been quite lucky there's so much that you can get involved in. I mean you do have to do mundane jobs, I’m not saying that you don’t, everyone has to, but knowing how to overcome that and organising it so it doesn’t take up the majority of your time and being able to say, ' Look, what really interests me, what's really going to get me through?' That's the only thing. So I don’t really see there being a disadvantage to it at all.

Interviewer:	What’s been the best and worst about your placement?

Subject:	The best and the worst ok - the worst: the fact that I get up at half-five each day, I commute for about an hour and a half to two hours to get here and I get home at seven.

Interviewer:	Where are you living?

Subject:	 [Area], so I’m at home - and then again I thought, 'Its just for a year, no hassle and it's not going to last forever, but it does mean that you can't do anything during the week, you're just absolutely exhausted and your weekend's over really quick, but some people actually live closer but they find all their money goes on rent and stuff, but the only down side is the commute. I won't be sorry to say bye to that, and getting up so early. The best thing I think is what I've learned about myself and how I deal with people and certain situations and tweaking my approach to tasks that sometimes might have frustrated me previously but I'm learning how to deal with it more effectively now, so on the positive - what someone can take from it personally.

Interviewer:	Did you say there was another student on placement here? Do you think that’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having other students on placement?

Subject:	I think there's actually another eight students, two of us are girls and the rest are boys. Like I said all of us are from an engineering background really and she's the only one that isn't. And it has been good, there's luckily a good set of people and sometimes we go out to lunch and stuff. The age range of the people here isn't that drastic that you’d feel left out, even though you do come up against all different ages, but it's not that kind of environment where you know they sit over there and they sit over there, it's not like that at all. The fact that other students are here so you can talk about, ‘oh what modules have you done’ and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’re all treated equally?

Subject:	Yeah I think so. Equally in terms of work or just in general?

Interviewer:	Yes. So do you think anyone has been given more or less responsibility or anything like that? 

Subject:	In a way that’s a difficult one to answer because working in different cells so it really depends on the demand of that cell but I don’t think yeah I don’t think its to the extent that someone’s coming out absolutely knackered and someone’s like ‘oh I’m bored’, kind of thing. 

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve been treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

Subject:	Yes. (laughing) They do make little digs about it, they do, you know that students don't do any work anyway and all that kind of stuff, it's nothing like harsh, its just meant in a jokey kind of way. But I think we do, we get the same amount of holidays, and if we are on site or anything to do with customers we’re treated exactly the same way, so I mean when we're dealing with customers, they don't actually know that we're students, so we aren't treated any differently.

Interviewer:	That’s good. I went somewhere where the student’s job title was something like ‘Assistant Trainee Student’.

Subject:	Oh no. Well luckily they tell us not to put that. 

Interviewer:	When you’ve been doing group work has there been any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	I'd describe it as like to a certain extent, and then depending on how the discussion goes, there's just elements that really like tick you off. I wouldn't say solely someone’s whole character, you’re just like ‘no, forget it.’, apart from one customer based in Italy recently, that no matter how many times you told him about his parts he refused to believe it, but that was just him being difficult. But it terms of group work, I don’t think so. 

Interviewer:	Have you been given a mentor at all?

Subject:	A lady I work with, she's kind of like my supervisor for that kind of work and I work along side her, but one of the undergraduates - no graduate students sorry, they're kind of responsible for students, and we do monthly presentations about what we've done and I think they are planning on doing a site visit when one of the power stations in [name], they are going to open up part of their unit, so that we can all go and see that, so

Interviewer:	Have you found that a good idea? 

Subject:	It's really weird because you just tend to - it is really relaxed you just tend to speak to whoever. You don't feel as though you have to go to that specific person and you can't speak to anyone else. Like this lady who I work alongside with, in a way she is my mentor or supervisor, but I can speak to my manager quite freely about anything that's going on as well as the graduates, so -

Interviewer:	So there are lots of different people that you go to for advice?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone who you would regard as a role model?

Subject:	Yes. There are a few people I'd say, definitely. There's a guy who's actually involved in sales, but he's a Chartered Electrical and Mechanical Engineer. So his approach and obviously he’s been through the academic route and some of these guys haven't necessarily done that, they've worked on the shop floor or come through different routes, so yes, it quite interesting like talking to him about stuff. And also like some of the production guys, how they organise themselves and their people, getting the parts and stuff like that, definitely.

Interviewer:	Ok. Has anyone from university been to visit you yet?

Subject:	Yes, my visiting tutor has. I think in November. I've got another visit due by the end of April.

Interviewer:	Did you know the lecturer that came to visit you?

Subject:	Yes, yes

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s a good idea having the visits?

Subject:	Yes it is because I think with [name] … [name] is the er, I've forgotten what she does, but you know she organises the … placement coordinator, that’s it. She is great with that kind of stuff, paperwork kind of stuff, but in terms of if you feel unsure what you should be getting involved in or stuff of a more engineeringy type, things really she can't help you with, she's not of that background. The visiting tutor, even if they don't visit or just if they don’t visit a lot is what I mean, just to have them so that you can get in contact with them and ask them stuff I think definitely because --

Interviewer:	Have you been in touch with them apart from the visits?

Subject:	Not really. But I think if I’d gone through the placement and not really kept my focus of making sure I got things out of it that I can relate to in my degree, so I can go back and say, 'Well I've learned more than how to programme things in Excel and stuff, then I would have. I lost my train of thought then. Yes if I'd gone through the whole of the year without keeping that focus, when you go back to uni, you don't know, because you have to write a dissertation for the DIS don't you, you don't know whether you've fulfilled the criteria, there's other stuff that you could have got involved in that you could talk about of a more engineering or technical nature that would be more relevant, especially since the year can contribute if you want to go on to be Chartered.

Interviewer:	Did you talk about your dissertation then?

Subject:	I don’t think I did because it was just in the early stages really so it was just to make sure that we were like just enjoying it, taking stuff in and getting involved in it and making sure that we were getting involved in training and things that will really count when we left. 

Interviewer:	Did they speak to your supervisor as well? 

Subject:	Yes, yes. 

Interviewer:	Would you be happy to go to the visiting tutor if you did have any problems? 

Subject:	Yes. I think it depends if it's more that you hate your placement I think you'd definitely speak to your tutor. If it's more personal like - I can' really think of an example, but not of any old issue I'd keep it straight to anything related to the course and any subject areas and not really personal. Any personal stuff I’d probably more likely to solve it myself (inaudible) and then obviously [placement co-ordinator] if there any problems with the placement itself.

Interviewer:	Are there appropriate facilities here for women? Toilets etc. Do you have to wear safety clothing? 

Subject:	We do have to wear overalls, but we're all supplied with boots or shoes if you like, goggles and everything.

Interviewer:	Do they always fit?

Subject:	Oh yes, yes. With the girls they waited until they actually got here and we ordered it, with the boys it was just a case of, 'We've got a spare set so there you go'. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that you want a career in engineering now?

Subject:	I think --

Interviewer:	Do you think the placement has changed your career ambitions?

Subject:	Not really, I was hoping it was just make me aware of some more things in the industry, because with engineering you just tend to think, I don't know, just engines or like the hard stuff, the oily stuff, you know getting messy and now that I've been involved in it, I mean I've heard previously that it is such a wide field and it's true, there is so much that you can get involved in and even if it wasn't in hard engineering itself or heavy engineering itself, you could take on a more business role, you could be out on site, leading like all the technical assistants when they are taking things apart, there's just so much that you could get involved in like I think it would be silly to rule it out to be quite honest. And like this is just the energy section, [company name] covers medical systems. On a business level there's like insurance, finance and things like that, the manufacture of like household goods there's so much that you could get involved in.

Interviewer:	So it helps you decide which area you want to go in? 

Subject:	 (Laughing) No, I think the fact that it's so broad is even worse, because I still can't focus on a particular area, but in a way I think that's good because I don't know what will happen when I leave uni, but I'll see something that may interest me and then after a while I might try something else and that opportunity's there, being involved in it definitely.

Interviewer:	Would you work for [company] when you graduate if they offered you a job?

Subject:	Yes, I would. Like I said again the opportunities that you have - but I haven't compared it to other companies what they'd offer - like say Graduate wise, but even though it's obviously –(inaudible). There is just so much to get involved in it would be silly not to.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the placement will help you get a job when you finish?

Subject:	Yes because I think, even when you go to an interview and you're selling yourself, whatever it is you're more aware of your skills and you how you really deal with things. You'll probably have a better idea of what you can and can't do, you won't just have a clouded view of it and say, ‘Oh I’ll give that a shot.’ You can be a bit realistic about it. I think yes, what you can take away from the whole year, what you might have learned, I think yes, I come back to it again and again, but how you deal with things, your approach to things.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will help you when you actually start doing work?

Subject:	You'll know what to expect it won't be such a shock to the system. It's not, it won’t be quite as daunting as you initially expected.

Interviewer:	Ok. Can you think of any occasions where you feel like you’re gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people or the outcome events or anything like that?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	Are people ever shocked to be dealing with a woman and not a man?

Subject:	No. I think any kind of shock that would happen here would be down to your personality, nothing to do with gender at all, nothing at all, it really isn't. Even if there was one woman working here it really wouldn't make much difference, it's all down to your personality and how you come across.

Interviewer:	Ok I have got some questions now, which are questions I asked you in the previous interview, just to see how you’re opinion has changed. So what five words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry? 

Subject:	Ok, I'd definitely say unglamorous, I'd say - unglamorous because – I would put it down to the environment its very to the point – it is very focussed, obviously you’ve nice people, but it's not so - I don't know how to describe it. You've got a job to do and you just try everything to get it done.

Interviewer:	Do you mean unglamourous image-wise?

Subject:	Yes, I think the image of it definitely, yes image-wise definitely, probably not - yes probably not, well actually in the industry itself it would be seen as that because sometimes well especially on the shop floor guys, unsociable hours and the things, the type of work they're doing is physical and it is taxing, its not yeah. No five words I am struggling. Right one last time, repeat the question just so I have got the –

Interviewer:	Can you give me five words that you would use to describe the characteristics of your field of engineering? 

Subject:	It is - I don't know whether I can put it in a word, but the opportunities are endless - whatever word relates to that. It is interesting - yes definitely very interesting. 

Interviewer:	From what you have told me probably very varied?

Subject:	What the type of work? (Yes) Yes, its definitely so varied I think just saying the word 'engineering' just doesn’t justify it, and I think that's probably what puts people off because when they hear the word, they just associate it with a certain environment and its just not that word at all. I think I'm gonna struggle to find five.

Interviewer:	That's alright. Would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	Only because there are a lot of men involved. I don't think it is. Yes just because maybe the effect of like men being together for so long whatever, it's just like a boys kind of thing but I really don’t think the environment is masculine. 

Interviewer:	There’s no reason why women …

Subject:	No. From what I've experienced here, it is fair so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are advantages or disadvantages then to being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	The only disadvantage, well not only, I think, people outside the industry, their perspective of you or their ideas about you. 

Interviewer:	Do you mean when you tell someone that you’re an engineer?

Subject:	Yes. Disdvantages? Maybe if you went into the field where you are on site and working unsociable hours there's not really, you wouldn't really think of women doing it. I know there was a lady that came over here from the States and she was down on the shop floor doing some welding, and it's not something that - over there it's quite common apparently, but over here you just wouldn’t hear of it and this is a twenty-four operation as well.

Interviewer:	You mentioned telling people you are an engineer. Have you had a particular reaction from people when you tell them that?

Subject:	Yes, the reaction is they go very quiet because I don't know if they because they know there's a lot of work involved they know it involves the sciences, they immediately assume, well sometimes they just have this vision of no personality, quite dull, boring, what might be expected because they know that from school science and maths was really boring, but that doesn't mean that the people are -

Interviewer:	Do you think that perception is the same for all engineers or do you think it’s worse if you’re a woman?

Subject:	I’d say all engineers and then it is worse if you're a woman because women are expected to - I mean women do use their brains all the time, they're in the media, they get executive roles, the characteristics of those women are similar to what would make them succeed in engineering, but yes there is that belief that a woman must be really butch and really masculine and you just wouldn't need to, you just still go about being say, you know, a lady yourself or a woman yourself.

Interviewer:	Do you think it matters that there aren’t more women in engineering?

Subject:	I'm not sure if 'matters' is the right way of putting it, I think the view of the industry as a whole could do with some tweaking, people’s perception of it is erm …

Interviewer:	Could do with an image makeover?

Subject:	Yes, definitely, I think probably the opportunities within it aren't really advertised or made aware as much as possible. It's really only if you've got the interest will you actually seek to make yourself aware of the opportunities available. Like, it could also be down to the culture as well because I know, I just said the media, but a lot of people I know are interested in getting into media, they see the video, they see that kind of stuff and all they can think of is that media is the way to go. Say, like the music industry - and not to say that it's bad, but that is not the only thing you can do and I think you can do so much with engineering and that - you know, I don't know how you'd go about trying to change the opinion of a whole nation. How would you go about readjusting someone's culture, because I think it is a culture thing and the idea of working hard in terms of like studying and things, because it is quite demanding, not necessarily mechanical but any type of engineering it is demanding, and even at uni when it comes to your social students that probably don’t have as many hours and they're always looking at the science and engineering and they just always seem to be working. That image in itself is just like I’d rather take the easy option so -

Interviewer:	Do you think that there will be more women in engineering in the future then? 

Subject:	It would be nice, it would be nice, it's a shame that it's divided up into men and women, I really - if that image kind of changed and it was just universal, I'm sure you'd get an abundance of women in.

Interviewer:	So you think if we need to get more women in, we need to change their opinion of what engineering is?

Subject:	Definitely, yes, change the current perception of engineering definitely and really see the advantages that are out there. All the types of things, whether it is actual hands-on engineering to maybe the designs, every single element, really needs to be like bright lights. In the same way that the media manages to do it and music videos. Look how good we are whatever, it's more or less the same thing. But it is hard because in schools it is seen that science and maths is really hardcore basically and it's really whether that individual wants to put the effort in, because especially from the course, if you don't have the motivation when it is really tough like when you feel the pressure on yourself maybe you find something a bit difficult, because you do get those moments. You feel as though there's so much that you need to take in and you just can't take it in. Yes. You can't force that on anyone, it is ... Obviously the benefits afterwards are brilliant, but the stuff that you had to kind of sacrifice whilst doing it, I don't know if it's gonna be that easy to persuade people. Because I know, I still believe the uni route is seen as the most popular, I really don't think a lot of people are keen on the apprenticeship route, even though sometimes it is the best route and I don't think one route's better than the other, because you might do the apprenticeship and the skills that you'll gain from the actual physical work in terms of 'Oh yes I read it in a book', you can use both skills really, and yes, that’s a disadvantage I think, because at uni I don't think you're doing as much hands on. You would do the same as an apprentice, but that compensates. 

Interviewer:	Ok. Have you had opportunities to travel while you’ve been here then? 

Subject:	There's a few that have come over, but there are opportunities to travel. The ones that have come up, I think there's only probably one recently, I don't think it was anything I could have really benefited from, I could have done exactly the same thing here, but I have had the chance to go out on site and to see an actual gas turbine, to crawl about in my overalls and stuff, so the opportunity to get out and do stuff, yes, but at the moment the opportunity to travel is there.

Interviewer:	Ok that’s everything, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The questions I’ve got today are about how you’re getting on on placement, and how you think it relates to your course and things like that. And there’s a few questions about gender stuff as well. So when did you start working for [company]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: When did I start here? It would have been middle of July last year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Can you tell me a bit about what [company] do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK. This division sort of deals with like power generation really, so energy also covers wind power and what else? Sorry, I can only think gas turbines at the moment, power generators because that’s what they do here. This site specifically comes under inspection and repair and this workshop inspects and repairs gas turbines in different frame sizes all across Europe and part of the Midland East as well. Gas turbines are used mainly for power generation, industrial applications and just like the national grid and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's relaxed, you don't feel any pressure at all, obviously like at this site particularly because it’s a workshop there are a lot of men about, but you don't feel excluded or at an advantage in any way, it is a relaxed place here. I don't know if you would have the same kind of environment like in a more corporate position, but here it’s really relaxed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok I have got some more questions about that later. (Ok.) How useful do you think your degree has been so far in the work that you are doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At the moment I haven't really had to use anything that I learnt from my degree. Maybe how I apply myself to doing jobs, like the organisation and keeping your focus and like the self-motivation thing which is kind of common with the degree as well because it is a bit hardcore, if I can say that. But that's because at the moment I'm in the more commercial role, but because I'm from an engineering background I want to get involved in more production stuff, so I’m going to spend some time with the guys and learn a bit more about the turbine itself and the components, which I have done already, but there's always more to learn. So I'd say at the moment, not much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that you wish you had learned at uni before you started the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In order to help me here? (Yes) Not really apart from I could have made myself a bit more familiar with AutoCad ‘cos that seems to be a popular programme used in the industry. But I don’t think they could have prepared me any better course wise or just personal skills wise, I think it’s just … Luckily it's one of those environments where it's good to be in that situation and learn what’s going on there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do anything about Health and Safety at Uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We might have done it briefly when we did our projects and we had to be involved in the workshop. I don’t think there was massive training.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had to do a lot of Health and Safety stuff here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. On my first day here we did Health and Safety, just in order to say that we could go on the shop floor. We couldn’t go anywhere without it. And recently we've been on the site, and because certain companies have their own on site Health and Safety you have to go through that before you can be allowed on the site, especially if you're going unescorted.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the Health and Safety stuff you learnt at uni helped when you got here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it's pretty much the same, but I suppose maybe there's greater risk on site because you're actually dealing with the actual turbines. They're going to tweak it somehow, so it's not going to change that much, but I think Health and Safety its one of those things that just because you've done it once doesn’t mean you should forget it. It should be done all the time, so that's not a problem at all, even if when you go through that with me its good to know it when you're in the actual environment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. How did you find the transition from education to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not a problem it was fine, I think because I did a foundation year I’d done an extra year at college I think I needed the year out just to see where it would all go, even though I haven’t really used much of what I’ve learnt so far. But, to see like an industry that actually involves engineering, it makes a change from just reading the text books all the time. (Yes) Its good to see it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve had to face any new issues at all, like dealing with different types of people or office politics, anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's been fine. I think it's good in a sense that depending on how you’re going to react to it, you'll learn a way of how to deal with it. Either you will stay focussed on what you're doing and not get involved in it, or you might be of the character that, you know, will get involved in it. I haven’t, I’ve been able to stay focused. You just get used to it really. So, what’s the word? You're not as vulnerable to the situation; you wise up to it and also, yes definitely, dealing with differently types of people. There are some people that might have the same background as you university wise, used to working in groups, just a different approach to things, and then obviously you've got the workshop guys that have a different set of skills, and knowing how to talk to everyone and deal with everyone, and not expecting them to, kind of like be psychic really, do you know what I mean? It’s just learning to deal with it. I don't think that's an element that you can get away or not get anywhere. Any new environment that you're , even though you've dealt with it before and you have those skills, you’re tested once again, so the test really is to keep doing it. But it’s never been a problem really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. How do you feel about going back to uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm really not looking forward to doing exams, it's been nice, the fact that - I don't know if my focus is better, but at work for the duration that you’re here, you can focus on work and at least you get that chance to switch off when you go home or at the weekends and at uni it just seems to be a never ending, up-hill struggle sometimes, so I'm enjoying having my year out kind of thing, and when it comes back to October, I will just deal with it then. I am not going to speed up the process. I want to enjoy my experience here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok What do you think are the main ways that work and university differ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way the deadlines, like something - whether you’ve have a long time to work on it or something’s come up like when units have gone through (forced altitude?) you need to, that’s like when they have had to shut them down unexpectedly, and certain information is needed on the spot. Well obviously like at uni you do have coursework and things but you kind of know how long you've got to do it. Yes like I said the fact that with work you can kind of leave work at work. You can switch off, you can actually leave. You feel as though you can detach from the situation and come back to work refreshed. I think your focus is better then as well because you're not thinking about it all time. Also I think in the workplace it's a lot to do with how you interact with people. We do get the opportunity to do a lot of teamwork or group work at uni, but it's just not the same. I can appreciate what they were trying to do and I’d still encourage them to do it, but in the workplace it's a totally different system.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I've thought about it, I think at university it seems like a real chore, a real hassle to work in a group, and at work it just seems like you've got this common goal, you are just trying to get each others ideas and obviously some people might know certain information and you need to retrieve that from them. And it does seem like you're working together like really with your aims in the same kind of framework. Yes the only way I can describe it in uni is like a chore. You think 'oh not group work again’ you think that can do it better in your own time by yourself, it would be great kind of thing. You don't have to be bothered with meetings and things like that whereas at work you've got to say (inaudible) in the same places, you do have other commitments, and it might be workplace, it might be outside but at work you can appreciate meetings more, getting together churning out your ideas, going away. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think at work you maybe have clearer roles within your teams?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. You pick up on like peoples skills and say yes they know how to best go about something or they know where to find out certain information. Yes, it is much easier, not that it’s discussed that ‘yes, you’ll do this and you’ll do this’, but it is clearer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there is anyway that group work at uni could be redesigned to reflect industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't know. At uni there seems to be more of a competitive edge, everybody, even though you are working in a group, the competitiveness is there more than in the workplace and there's always someone trying to be the leader to lead the group, instead of how about everyone just taking even responsibility, so I can't think how you could implement that but from the group work that I have done, I think that’s probably one of the things that could make team work more effective.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think that you’ve found being at uni is a more competitive environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you still think that there are benefits from doing group work at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. You do need to know how to work with people that aren't just your friends and you say 'oh do you know I'm going to have a lie in, can you do that for me' definitely needs to be done. I'd suggest it would be really good if students doing it got a chance to do a placement, went ahead a did a placement to really see where it fits in. Because I think probably in a uni environment you might think that you get on well with people, but in a work situation, you are actually thrown together, you can't really afford to have conflict that you would normally and fly off the handle. It’s really not like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you will get on better working in a group when you go back?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Well last year I found myself getting really frustrated at things, like trying to get your point across and then obviously if you've got someone that's really strong about their view about something. Whereas yeah definitely here you feel you can give your idea, it can be reviewed and it's a bit fairer. I still think there is competitiveness here, because you've got your production people and your commercial people and there's a bit of a battle between them 'Oh you haven't passed me the right information on’ and that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that between departments then? (Yes.) Ok. Do [company] employ many women here then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They do employ women, I don't know whether you'd regard it as many. I'll see if I can count – I believe it might be 5, but let me check. Possibly 6, but I'd say 3 of those are more of an admin position, 1 just happens to be another student, but then again she's coming in from a marketing economics background. A student just like me. There's another lady here she was at, she did a degree in material science, but she's still in a commercial role and then there's myself. So yes they do employ them, but not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Do the company have a structure or programme in place for placement students to follow?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In terms of you are given responsibility, there is a job to do, it might be assisting one of the managers with what they do. You have the responsibility of checking out details of things but it's not too structured, which is a good thing because there's a lot of stuff that's going on here and it is a big organisation and if there is anything that you find interesting and want to get involved in, all you have to do is say and it can happen, so that is good. I think it's important that you've got the interest there. You kind of go into your placement knowing what you want to take out from it. It can be like a brief thing it doesn't have to be so specific ‘I want to learn how to use that piece of equipment’, but you need some sort of plan when you go for it, and I think that, it's 50/50 that the company put a structure there for you but also for you to be able to say actually, I think I'd benefit more from this, you know I've not giving it my best or you’re not getting the best out of me while I'm stuck here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have appraisals or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, but my Commercial Manager, he's based up in Scotland cos’ he works from home, but when he's down he always takes, say half an hour, sometimes even more, to find out how you’re doing, if there’s anything that’s bothering you, if there's anything that you want to do. Its not really an appraisal but there is kind of that check up on you to make sure that you're not just sat here bawling your eyes because your bored like rigid kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Has your role in the company involved what you expected?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know, in a way no, I thought I'd thought I'd be learning a bit more about the technology, a bit more about the engineering side of things. It's difficult here cos’ most of the engineering is done out in the States and here it's mainly processing and production and things like that, but even on a production level there's a lot to learn from it, so that's why I really really want to get into that side. Initially it didn't bother me too much because obviously a new environment, I've not been in like this kind of industry before, and you're trying to get to grips with your job and the ways of doing things, so I was quite happy just to do that. At the same time I did like have an interest in coming down on the shop floor and enquire myself. At the beginning it wasn't so specific, not that they hadn't planned what to do for me as a role, but in a way that flexibility is there. But I think I would have like to spend a bit more time on the production side of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely not too little. I'd say, yes, not to feel the pressure wise, but no definitely, like yes there’s certain jobs that you’re left to kind of take care of. Obviously people are about if you need to ask questions, you don't feel as though you have to go through it alone and if something goes wrong it’s all your fault.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you feel like you’re in a supportive environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes definitely. I think that for the experience that we have, just coming in from university, it's not an insulting level of like responsibility but I think it’s a good level.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. How would you summarise the experience so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So far? I'm definitely glad that I've done it. I think I wouldn't have been able to take from it if I'd just stayed at university. Now I realise, I wasn’t of the idea of doing a placement anyway, but I think it's just as valuable as doing your degree and it's one thing knowing all the stuff, which is great, but being able to apply it and communicate that across to people is so important and even how you deal with things in certain environments where maybe previously you would have like got annoyed so it's a lot to do with how you respond to things, how you go about - yes personal things. And also it gives you more confidence, because a lot of the time like particularly at uni, well anywhere really, you always feel as though there's always going to be someone doing a better job than you are, and at uni I think the pressure really is there obviously because you really think that you're trying your hardest and maybe it's just the way that you're applying yourself to it. Yes you can really put the pressure on yourself a lot, and being here, in a way uses all your skills, not just what you've learned out of a text book or at a lecture, but how you are as a person, it's like you're using one hundred per cent of you more or less. The confidence that you can take from that when you're going back into your final year I think it will help a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s been a positive experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Drawbacks? The only drawbacks, I suppose it depends on the type of person is they’re going to look on it as being an extra year at uni or if they don’t have the - what's the word - I can't think of the word but if your like in your placement, you're not exactly stimulated but you need to find areas or see how you going to solve this problem, how you’re going to motivate yourself. 'What is there that’s going to interest me?' I think I've been quite lucky there's so much that you can get involved in. I mean you do have to do mundane jobs, I’m not saying that you don’t, everyone has to, but knowing how to overcome that and organising it so it doesn’t take up the majority of your time and being able to say, ' Look, what really interests me, what's really going to get me through?' That's the only thing. So I don’t really see there being a disadvantage to it at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What’s been the best and worst about your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best and the worst ok - the worst: the fact that I get up at half-five each day, I commute for about an hour and a half to two hours to get here and I get home at seven.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Where are you living?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Area], so I’m at home - and then again I thought, 'Its just for a year, no hassle and it's not going to last forever, but it does mean that you can't do anything during the week, you're just absolutely exhausted and your weekend's over really quick, but some people actually live closer but they find all their money goes on rent and stuff, but the only down side is the commute. I won't be sorry to say bye to that, and getting up so early. The best thing I think is what I've learned about myself and how I deal with people and certain situations and tweaking my approach to tasks that sometimes might have frustrated me previously but I'm learning how to deal with it more effectively now, so on the positive - what someone can take from it personally.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you say there was another student on placement here? Do you think that’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having other students on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there's actually another eight students, two of us are girls and the rest are boys. Like I said all of us are from an engineering background really and she's the only one that isn't. And it has been good, there's luckily a good set of people and sometimes we go out to lunch and stuff. The age range of the people here isn't that drastic that you’d feel left out, even though you do come up against all different ages, but it's not that kind of environment where you know they sit over there and they sit over there, it's not like that at all. The fact that other students are here so you can talk about, ‘oh what modules have you done’ and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’re all treated equally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I think so. Equally in terms of work or just in general?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. So do you think anyone has been given more or less responsibility or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way that’s a difficult one to answer because working in different cells so it really depends on the demand of that cell but I don’t think yeah I don’t think its to the extent that someone’s coming out absolutely knackered and someone’s like ‘oh I’m bored’, kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. (laughing) They do make little digs about it, they do, you know that students don't do any work anyway and all that kind of stuff, it's nothing like harsh, its just meant in a jokey kind of way. But I think we do, we get the same amount of holidays, and if we are on site or anything to do with customers we’re treated exactly the same way, so I mean when we're dealing with customers, they don't actually know that we're students, so we aren't treated any differently.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s good. I went somewhere where the student’s job title was something like ‘Assistant Trainee Student’.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh no. Well luckily they tell us not to put that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you’ve been doing group work has there been any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd describe it as like to a certain extent, and then depending on how the discussion goes, there's just elements that really like tick you off. I wouldn't say solely someone’s whole character, you’re just like ‘no, forget it.’, apart from one customer based in Italy recently, that no matter how many times you told him about his parts he refused to believe it, but that was just him being difficult. But it terms of group work, I don’t think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been given a mentor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A lady I work with, she's kind of like my supervisor for that kind of work and I work along side her, but one of the undergraduates - no graduate students sorry, they're kind of responsible for students, and we do monthly presentations about what we've done and I think they are planning on doing a site visit when one of the power stations in [name], they are going to open up part of their unit, so that we can all go and see that, so

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you found that a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's really weird because you just tend to - it is really relaxed you just tend to speak to whoever. You don't feel as though you have to go to that specific person and you can't speak to anyone else. Like this lady who I work alongside with, in a way she is my mentor or supervisor, but I can speak to my manager quite freely about anything that's going on as well as the graduates, so -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So there are lots of different people that you go to for advice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone who you would regard as a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. There are a few people I'd say, definitely. There's a guy who's actually involved in sales, but he's a Chartered Electrical and Mechanical Engineer. So his approach and obviously he’s been through the academic route and some of these guys haven't necessarily done that, they've worked on the shop floor or come through different routes, so yes, it quite interesting like talking to him about stuff. And also like some of the production guys, how they organise themselves and their people, getting the parts and stuff like that, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Has anyone from university been to visit you yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, my visiting tutor has. I think in November. I've got another visit due by the end of April.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know the lecturer that came to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yes

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s a good idea having the visits?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it is because I think with [name] … [name] is the er, I've forgotten what she does, but you know she organises the … placement coordinator, that’s it. She is great with that kind of stuff, paperwork kind of stuff, but in terms of if you feel unsure what you should be getting involved in or stuff of a more engineeringy type, things really she can't help you with, she's not of that background. The visiting tutor, even if they don't visit or just if they don’t visit a lot is what I mean, just to have them so that you can get in contact with them and ask them stuff I think definitely because --

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been in touch with them apart from the visits?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. But I think if I’d gone through the placement and not really kept my focus of making sure I got things out of it that I can relate to in my degree, so I can go back and say, 'Well I've learned more than how to programme things in Excel and stuff, then I would have. I lost my train of thought then. Yes if I'd gone through the whole of the year without keeping that focus, when you go back to uni, you don't know, because you have to write a dissertation for the DIS don't you, you don't know whether you've fulfilled the criteria, there's other stuff that you could have got involved in that you could talk about of a more engineering or technical nature that would be more relevant, especially since the year can contribute if you want to go on to be Chartered.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you talk about your dissertation then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think I did because it was just in the early stages really so it was just to make sure that we were like just enjoying it, taking stuff in and getting involved in it and making sure that we were getting involved in training and things that will really count when we left.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did they speak to your supervisor as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you be happy to go to the visiting tutor if you did have any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I think it depends if it's more that you hate your placement I think you'd definitely speak to your tutor. If it's more personal like - I can' really think of an example, but not of any old issue I'd keep it straight to anything related to the course and any subject areas and not really personal. Any personal stuff I’d probably more likely to solve it myself (inaudible) and then obviously [placement co-ordinator] if there any problems with the placement itself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there appropriate facilities here for women? Toilets etc. Do you have to wear safety clothing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We do have to wear overalls, but we're all supplied with boots or shoes if you like, goggles and everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do they always fit?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yes, yes. With the girls they waited until they actually got here and we ordered it, with the boys it was just a case of, 'We've got a spare set so there you go'.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you want a career in engineering now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think --

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the placement has changed your career ambitions?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, I was hoping it was just make me aware of some more things in the industry, because with engineering you just tend to think, I don't know, just engines or like the hard stuff, the oily stuff, you know getting messy and now that I've been involved in it, I mean I've heard previously that it is such a wide field and it's true, there is so much that you can get involved in and even if it wasn't in hard engineering itself or heavy engineering itself, you could take on a more business role, you could be out on site, leading like all the technical assistants when they are taking things apart, there's just so much that you could get involved in like I think it would be silly to rule it out to be quite honest. And like this is just the energy section, [company name] covers medical systems. On a business level there's like insurance, finance and things like that, the manufacture of like household goods there's so much that you could get involved in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it helps you decide which area you want to go in?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (Laughing) No, I think the fact that it's so broad is even worse, because I still can't focus on a particular area, but in a way I think that's good because I don't know what will happen when I leave uni, but I'll see something that may interest me and then after a while I might try something else and that opportunity's there, being involved in it definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you work for [company] when you graduate if they offered you a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I would. Like I said again the opportunities that you have - but I haven't compared it to other companies what they'd offer - like say Graduate wise, but even though it's obviously –(inaudible). There is just so much to get involved in it would be silly not to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the placement will help you get a job when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes because I think, even when you go to an interview and you're selling yourself, whatever it is you're more aware of your skills and you how you really deal with things. You'll probably have a better idea of what you can and can't do, you won't just have a clouded view of it and say, ‘Oh I’ll give that a shot.’ You can be a bit realistic about it. I think yes, what you can take away from the whole year, what you might have learned, I think yes, I come back to it again and again, but how you deal with things, your approach to things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will help you when you actually start doing work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You'll know what to expect it won't be such a shock to the system. It's not, it won’t be quite as daunting as you initially expected.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Can you think of any occasions where you feel like you’re gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people or the outcome events or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are people ever shocked to be dealing with a woman and not a man?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I think any kind of shock that would happen here would be down to your personality, nothing to do with gender at all, nothing at all, it really isn't. Even if there was one woman working here it really wouldn't make much difference, it's all down to your personality and how you come across.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok I have got some questions now, which are questions I asked you in the previous interview, just to see how you’re opinion has changed. So what five words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ok, I'd definitely say unglamorous, I'd say - unglamorous because – I would put it down to the environment its very to the point – it is very focussed, obviously you’ve nice people, but it's not so - I don't know how to describe it. You've got a job to do and you just try everything to get it done.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you mean unglamourous image-wise?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think the image of it definitely, yes image-wise definitely, probably not - yes probably not, well actually in the industry itself it would be seen as that because sometimes well especially on the shop floor guys, unsociable hours and the things, the type of work they're doing is physical and it is taxing, its not yeah. No five words I am struggling. Right one last time, repeat the question just so I have got the –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you give me five words that you would use to describe the characteristics of your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is - I don't know whether I can put it in a word, but the opportunities are endless - whatever word relates to that. It is interesting - yes definitely very interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: From what you have told me probably very varied?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What the type of work? (Yes) Yes, its definitely so varied I think just saying the word 'engineering' just doesn’t justify it, and I think that's probably what puts people off because when they hear the word, they just associate it with a certain environment and its just not that word at all. I think I'm gonna struggle to find five.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's alright. Would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Only because there are a lot of men involved. I don't think it is. Yes just because maybe the effect of like men being together for so long whatever, it's just like a boys kind of thing but I really don’t think the environment is masculine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: There’s no reason why women …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. From what I've experienced here, it is fair so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are advantages or disadvantages then to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The only disadvantage, well not only, I think, people outside the industry, their perspective of you or their ideas about you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you mean when you tell someone that you’re an engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Disdvantages? Maybe if you went into the field where you are on site and working unsociable hours there's not really, you wouldn't really think of women doing it. I know there was a lady that came over here from the States and she was down on the shop floor doing some welding, and it's not something that - over there it's quite common apparently, but over here you just wouldn’t hear of it and this is a twenty-four operation as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You mentioned telling people you are an engineer. Have you had a particular reaction from people when you tell them that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, the reaction is they go very quiet because I don't know if they because they know there's a lot of work involved they know it involves the sciences, they immediately assume, well sometimes they just have this vision of no personality, quite dull, boring, what might be expected because they know that from school science and maths was really boring, but that doesn't mean that the people are -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that perception is the same for all engineers or do you think it’s worse if you’re a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say all engineers and then it is worse if you're a woman because women are expected to - I mean women do use their brains all the time, they're in the media, they get executive roles, the characteristics of those women are similar to what would make them succeed in engineering, but yes there is that belief that a woman must be really butch and really masculine and you just wouldn't need to, you just still go about being say, you know, a lady yourself or a woman yourself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it matters that there aren’t more women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm not sure if 'matters' is the right way of putting it, I think the view of the industry as a whole could do with some tweaking, people’s perception of it is erm …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Could do with an image makeover?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely, I think probably the opportunities within it aren't really advertised or made aware as much as possible. It's really only if you've got the interest will you actually seek to make yourself aware of the opportunities available. Like, it could also be down to the culture as well because I know, I just said the media, but a lot of people I know are interested in getting into media, they see the video, they see that kind of stuff and all they can think of is that media is the way to go. Say, like the music industry - and not to say that it's bad, but that is not the only thing you can do and I think you can do so much with engineering and that - you know, I don't know how you'd go about trying to change the opinion of a whole nation. How would you go about readjusting someone's culture, because I think it is a culture thing and the idea of working hard in terms of like studying and things, because it is quite demanding, not necessarily mechanical but any type of engineering it is demanding, and even at uni when it comes to your social students that probably don’t have as many hours and they're always looking at the science and engineering and they just always seem to be working. That image in itself is just like I’d rather take the easy option so -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there will be more women in engineering in the future then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It would be nice, it would be nice, it's a shame that it's divided up into men and women, I really - if that image kind of changed and it was just universal, I'm sure you'd get an abundance of women in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think if we need to get more women in, we need to change their opinion of what engineering is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, yes, change the current perception of engineering definitely and really see the advantages that are out there. All the types of things, whether it is actual hands-on engineering to maybe the designs, every single element, really needs to be like bright lights. In the same way that the media manages to do it and music videos. Look how good we are whatever, it's more or less the same thing. But it is hard because in schools it is seen that science and maths is really hardcore basically and it's really whether that individual wants to put the effort in, because especially from the course, if you don't have the motivation when it is really tough like when you feel the pressure on yourself maybe you find something a bit difficult, because you do get those moments. You feel as though there's so much that you need to take in and you just can't take it in. Yes. You can't force that on anyone, it is ... Obviously the benefits afterwards are brilliant, but the stuff that you had to kind of sacrifice whilst doing it, I don't know if it's gonna be that easy to persuade people. Because I know, I still believe the uni route is seen as the most popular, I really don't think a lot of people are keen on the apprenticeship route, even though sometimes it is the best route and I don't think one route's better than the other, because you might do the apprenticeship and the skills that you'll gain from the actual physical work in terms of 'Oh yes I read it in a book', you can use both skills really, and yes, that’s a disadvantage I think, because at uni I don't think you're doing as much hands on. You would do the same as an apprentice, but that compensates.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Have you had opportunities to travel while you’ve been here then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There's a few that have come over, but there are opportunities to travel. The ones that have come up, I think there's only probably one recently, I don't think it was anything I could have really benefited from, I could have done exactly the same thing here, but I have had the chance to go out on site and to see an actual gas turbine, to crawl about in my overalls and stuff, so the opportunity to get out and do stuff, yes, but at the moment the opportunity to travel is there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok that’s everything, thank you very much.
